newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania, donors welcome debt relief agreement.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania, donors welcome debt relief agreement.

text.p: Tanzanian officials and major donors welcomed on Friday a decision earlier this week by the Paris Club of creditor nations to give the East African nation its most generous terms for debt reduction.
"We are very grateful for this quite substantial debt relief," Finance Minister Daniel Yona told Reuters. But he added the government faced a tough task in sticking to its economic reforms.
"This (Paris Club decision) is only one of our goals we have set. But now we have to keep up with the payment which is left."
He said the government most importantly aimed to increase revenue collection, keep spending at a minimum, privatise ailing parastatals and cut the number of civil servants.
The Paris Club agreement which was announced on Wednesday allowed reduction on debt repayments of up to 67 percent for Tanzania under the so-called "Naples terms" of debt relief.
The resident representative of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said total debt relief would be worth $1 billion.
"Tanzania did very well at the meeting and achieved debt rescheduling of $1.7 billion of which $1 billion was completely knocked off," Festus Osunsade said.
Creditor countries agreed they could meet by the end of 1999 to consider any reduction in Tanzania's stock of debt.
They could also undertake debt for nature, debt for aid, debt for equity swaps or other local currency swaps on up to 20 percent of the debt concerned, the Paris Club added.
"This is very positive. It's a major step forward," said a senior representative of a major foreign donor to Tanzania.
World Bank representative Ron Brigish said the decision was a major pat on the shoulder for the government of President Benjamin Mkapa and its tough economic policies.
"It's another sign of approval for Tanzania. It helps regularise relations with most donors and this is very important. It's a signal...Tanzania is now back in the fold," he said.
The IMF approved a new package of loans worth $234 million for Tanzania in November, the first IMF support since 1992.
